    "abstract": "Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a standard architectural response to unreliability in legal AI, yet high-profile failures, including fabricated citations submitted to courts and anachronistic legal content presented as current, continue to appear across jurisdictions. We argue that these failures are not residual confabulations to be eliminated by scaling language models, but symptoms of an architectural mismatch between probabilistic retrieval and the hierarchical, temporal, and institutional structure of legal knowledge. We develop the argument in three moves. First, we articulate the ontological commitment of legal knowledge as a triad of properties derivable from classical legal theory: hierarchical and mereological structure, diachronic dynamism under operational closure, and causal traceability of institutional provenance grounded in the duty of justification. Second, we identify three corresponding pathologies of retrieval (mereological blindness, diachronic blindness, and causal opacity), each developed with an operational definition, a failure mechanism, a canonical example, and detection criteria for diagnostic use. Third, we review the state of the art through this lens, showing that existing approaches address these requirements unevenly and do not yet compose into a paradigm that treats them as co-constitutive. From this analysis we derive four architectural commitments that characterize the deterministic-by-design direction for legal retrieval: ontological primacy, event reification, bitemporal correctness, and deterministic interaction protocols. The framework concerns quaestio juris (which norms apply and in what state) rather than the downstream tasks that act on identified norms, and addresses legislative and constitutional retrieval primarily, with interpretive time as an explicit extension.",

{ "paper": { "id": "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6459080", "title": "Nor-CaseHOLD: A Retrieval Benchmark for Norwegian Legal AI", "authors": [ "Bendik Eeg-Henriksen" ], "year": 2026, "published": null, "venue": null, "url": "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6459080", "pdf_url": null, "abstract": "

This paper presents two contributions to Norwegian legal NLP: Norwegian Legal BERT, a domain-adapted BERT model built by continuing masked language model pretraining of NbAiLab/nb-bert-base using 9,140 Norwegian legal documents; and Nor-CaseHOLD, a legal retrieval benchmark built from 1,244 documents — 627 Supreme Court (Høyesterett) decisions and 617 Skatteetaten bindende forhåndsuttalelser (BFU) — each paired with its official summary. 

To the author's knowledge, Norwegian Legal BERT is the first open-source domain-adapted Norwegian legal language model, and Nor-CaseHOLD is the first Norwegian open-source legal retrieval benchmark.

So far nine retrieval methods have been benchmarked using Nor-CaseHOLD, including Norwegian Legal BERT. These cover sparse retrieval (BM25, TF-IDF), dense encoders (Norwegian Legal BERT, NB-BERT-base, mBERT, multilingual MiniLM), structural baselines (Lead-5), and oracle upper bounds (greedy and sequential). Two additional experiments — hybrid BM25+dense scoring and cross-encoder reranking — were also tested. All results include bootstrap confidence intervals and pairwise significance tests. 

Key finding so far is that among non-oracle methods, sparse retrieval dominates the benchmark with BM25 and TF-IDF achieving the highest ROUGE-1 clocking in at 47.49 and 47.85 respectively — this is a common finding across jurisdictions, and our benchmarks seem to reinforce that point. Neither hybrid scoring nor cross-encoder reranking improved over pure BM25. As for dense encoders, Norwegian Legal BERT (38.40) outperforms NB-BERT-base (37.28, p < 0.001) and mBERT (37.34, p < 0.01), confirming that pretraining improves performance.

Rankings are consistent across Høyesterett and BFU data, indicating that findings apply across different types of legal documents. Both Norwegian Legal BERT and Nor-CaseHOLD are publicly available on HuggingFace and GitHub under open licences.

future_work: Section 6 Research Agenda: interpretive time and the doctrinal dimension; evaluation methodology for deterministic retrieval; cross-jurisdictional portability
key_assumptions: Legal knowledge is hierarchical/mereological, diachronically dynamic and causally traceable, and these properties are translatable into retrieval requirements
The relevant task is quaestio juris (which norms apply and in what state), primarily legislative and constitutional retrieval
Deterministic-by-design retrieval (ontology, event reification, bitemporal correctness, deterministic protocols) is the appropriate direction
limitations: Explicitly no benchmarked empirical comparison; contribution is formal and diagnostic
Scope limited to quaestio juris and legislative/constitutional retrieval; case law treated as an extension; interpretive time deferred to future work
input.main_contribution: An ontological framing of legal knowledge and a three-pathology diagnostic (mereological blindness, diachronic blindness, causal opacity) for legal retrieval, from which four architectural commitments are derived (ontological primacy, event reification, bitemporal correctness, deterministic interaction protocols).
input.method: Conceptual/position framework grounded in classical legal theory plus a pathology-organized critical review of existing legal retrieval approaches; no retrieval algorithm, no empirical study.
metrics: none reported (defines detection criteria for pathologies instead)
input.problem: Legal RAG failures (anachronistic content, fabricated citations, structural incompleteness) are argued to be symptoms of an architectural mismatch between probabilistic retrieval and the hierarchical, temporal and institutional structure of legal knowledge, rather than residual confabulations to be fixed by scaling.

relation_to_idea.basis: Full text read: the paper names the same temporal pathology ('diachronic blindness' = failure to reconstruct the state of norms at a point in time, including statutory evolution through amendments) and the same validity-vs-transaction-time requirement, but proposes no retrieval mechanism, no temporal score and no benchmark, and explicitly reports no empirical comparison.
relation_to_idea.conceptual_difference: It is a diagnostic/position framework prescribing a deterministic-by-design, neuro-symbolic, bitemporal architecture for quaestio juris, whereas the proposal is a lightweight post-hoc temporal re-ranking term evaluated empirically. The paper pre-empts the conceptual claim that legal retrieval must respect valid time rather than recency, but does not deliver a measured retrieval component or a version-level retrieval benchmark.

input.results: No empirical results. Argues that existing approaches address the requirements unevenly and do not compose into a paradigm treating them as co-constitutive.

benchmarks: LEGAL-LINK-EU (L2-EU), a new legal multiple-choice benchmark
baselines: Multiple open LLMs compared (e.g., GPT-OSS 120B, GPT-OSS 20B, Ministral-3 14B, Llama-3.1 8B) and medical-domain baselines
datasets: LEGAL-LINK-EU: legal MCQA encoding temporal validity and normative relationships between EU normative acts
A medical reference dataset for domain comparison
future_work: not captured in the sections read
key_assumptions: Legal truth is contingent on jurisdiction, temporal validity and authority hierarchy
Multiple-choice diagnosis over normative-act relationships isolates legal grounding without requiring document comprehension
limitations: Benchmark is multiple-choice and deliberately independent of direct access to source text, so it does not test retrieval of versioned passages
Focus is model robustness/sycophancy rather than retrieval ranking
Static set of normative relationships; no near-duplicate successive versions of the same clause
input.main_contribution: LEGAL-LINK-EU, a legal benchmark encoding temporal validity and normative relationships, plus a comparative diagnostic showing legal LLMs (unlike medical ones) fail to judge when retrieved citations are useful, are overconfident under authoritative perturbations, and worsen with scale.
input.method: A four-axis comparative diagnostic (knowledge recall, grounding, confidence, robustness) evaluating LLMs on a new legal multiple-choice benchmark that encodes temporal validity and normative relationships, contrasted with a matched medical reference domain.
input.problem: LLMs are expected to show legal competence by analogy to medicine, but legal truth is contingent on jurisdiction, temporal validity and authority hierarchy; models appear unable to determine when retrieved citations are applicable and valid.

relation_to_idea.basis: Full text read: the benchmark explicitly encodes temporal validity in the legal domain, which overlaps with the proposed benchmark's target property, but it is MCQA and explicitly independent of source-text access, so it does not evaluate version-aware retrieval or near-duplicate amended clauses.
relation_to_idea.conceptual_difference: It measures LLM reasoning/robustness about legal effects of normative acts, not retrieval ranking over versioned text; there is no base retriever, no temporal relevance term, and no passage-level validity. It nonetheless occupies the claim 'a legal benchmark encoding temporal validity exists'.

input.results: Sharp domain asymmetry: medical LLMs benefit from verified sources while legal LLMs struggle to assess when retrieved citations are useful or misleading, show overconfidence in perturbed contexts, and increased scale amplifies the tendency.

datasets: curated legal document corpus (details not stated in abstract)
key_assumptions: A legal ontology can act as an active control layer over retrieval rather than only as background knowledge
Jurisdiction, topic, lifecycle status and temporal validity are computable properties of legal sources
limitations: Full text not accessible (publisher returned HTTP 403); judged from abstract only
Ontology- and rule-based governance rather than a scored temporal relevance term
No empirical metrics or benchmark reported in the abstract
input.main_contribution: An ontology-governed legal RAG architecture that filters sources by jurisdiction, topic, lifecycle status and temporal validity before retrieval, validates answers against approved, valid legal sources after generation, and records an audit trail.
input.method: Use a legal ontology as an active control layer: pre-retrieval filtering of legal sources by jurisdiction, topic, lifecycle status and temporal validity; post-generation validation of evidential support, citation validity, jurisdictional boundaries and safety/privacy; audit-trail logging.
input.problem: Standard RAG over legal corpora does not guarantee that retrieved sources are legally valid, up to date, applicable to the correct jurisdiction, or safe, so answers may hallucinate authority or rely on outdated rules.

relation_to_idea.basis: Abstract states that sources are filtered by 'temporal validity' before retrieval as an active control layer, which overlaps with the proposal's legality/validity component and its pluggable-layer framing; however it is ontology/rule based and reports no retrieval scoring or benchmark.
relation_to_idea.conceptual_difference: Implements validity as a hard ontology-driven admission filter plus post-hoc rule validation for governance and audit, not as a graded temporal relevance term combined with semantic similarity, and it targets trustworthy/auditable legal QA rather than measuring time-specific retrieval accuracy on amended versions.

input.description: Two retrieved legal-domain works already prescribe validity-aware retrieval (bitemporal correctness; ontology filtering by temporal validity) and a legal benchmark already encodes temporal validity. It is unclear whether a lightweight post-hoc temporal re-ranking study can be positioned as a distinct contribution against this line, or whether it is subsumed by deterministic-by-design legal retrieval. Resolving this determines whether to refine the contribution, change the hypothesis toward version-level contamination measurement, or abandon the direction.
input.question: Given that validity-aware legal retrieval is already prescribed and partially implemented, can a post-hoc temporal re-ranking component still be positioned as a distinct contribution, or is the remaining defensible delta only version-level contamination measurement on near-duplicate amended clauses?
input.rationale: The challenge search found the validity/bitemporal framing and a temporal-validity-filtering legal RAG already published, while the closest legal framework paper reports no empirical comparison, leaving measurement rather than concept as the apparent residual gap.

Let me write the summary.

I challenged U008 by searching for retrieval-agnostic temporal re-ranking, amended-statute benchmarks, and bi-temporal legal retrieval, then reading full texts of two decisive new papers; the verdict is **holds** — the assessment is reinforced rather than refuted, because the legal-retrieval literature already frames the requirement as bitemporal valid-time vs transaction-time correctness ("diachronic blindness", "bitemporal correctness"), a legal benchmark encoding temporal validity already exists (LEGAL-LINK-EU), and a legal RAG system already filters sources by temporal validity, leaving only the version-level contamination evaluation plus cross-retriever demonstration as untested.

I recorded seven new claims (C012–C018) with verified quotes covering those findings, added full-text analyses of the three new papers, marked U008 partially resolved with the narrowed distinctions, upgraded the feasibility uncertainty U003 (ELI validity dates exist) to partially resolved, and added U009 on whether a post-hoc temporal re-ranking study is still positionable as a distinct contribution.
